stimulus.text:
| Group | Response to the Declaration |
| African Americans | Its natural-rights language seemed to challenge slavery. Jefferson's first draft blamed slavery on Britain, but Congress removed that passage. Some enslaved people fled to the British; some in the North won freedom by serving in the militia or the Continental Army. |
| Native Americans | Most supported the British, fearing the land hunger of the new nation. |
| Women | Revolutionary ideals inspired the idea of republican motherhood: women would educate their sons to be citizens of the republic, so mothers themselves needed education. |

books.section: B. Common Sense, the Declaration of Independence, and Republican Self-Government

stem: Why did most Native Americans support the British during the Revolutionary War?

options.text: They feared the land hunger of the new American nation
They had been promised seats in Parliament if Britain won
options.misconception: No seats in Parliament were promised to Native peoples. The passage names a different reason.

options.text: They had fought alongside British troops in the French and Indian War
options.misconception: Background: most Native peoples in the Ohio Valley had allied with the French, not the British, in the earlier war.

options.text: They agreed with the Declaration's claim that all men are created equal
options.misconception: Agreement with the Declaration would point toward the Americans, not the British.

rationales.A: The table says it plainly: most Native Americans supported the British because they feared the land hunger of the new nation. An expanding republic threatened their land more than a distant king did.
rationales.B: Parliamentary seats were never offered to Native peoples. The reason in the table is land.
rationales.C: Native alliances in the French and Indian War were split — the Iroquois stood with Britain, while Ohio Valley and Great Lakes peoples stood with France.
rationales.D: The Declaration's equality claim would favor the American side. Native support went to Britain out of fear of American expansion.
rationales.general:
1. Read the table's row. Most Native Americans supported the British.
2. Read the reason beside it. Fear of the land hunger of the new nation.
3. Follow the logic. An expanding American nation meant settlers taking Native land — Britain looked like the lesser danger.
Remember: people choose sides by asking who threatens them most — for Native peoples, it was the land-hungry new nation.
